items.title: Marvel Snap's Draft mode is a limited-time breath of fresh air
items.content:
Feature Preview Modojo @ Shacknews Marvel Snap's Draft mode is a limited-time breath of fresh air Marvel Snap's upcoming Draft mode is such a refreshing shift from the meta that you'll wish it could stay around longer.

The announcement of the August 2026 season of Marvel Snap was an exciting one for a few reasons. First, it marked the return of Second Dinner co-founder Ben Brode to the reveal videos after several months away. Second, Brode teased a major new reveal for Marvel Snap. That reveal is a limited-time game mode called Draft. Draft shakes up the standard Marvel Snap formula in some big ways. I recently had a chance to try it out and I walked away hoping that Second Dinner would consider making Draft a more permanent mode.

Marvel Snap's Draft mode tasks players with putting together a set of ten cards, which will expand to a full 12-card deck over the course of a run. Players begin by selecting a Starter Set, all of which follow an archetype like Swarm, Ramp, or Control. One of the Starter Set cards will appear front-and-center, appearing as the lead card to build around. For my session, I wouldn't be a toxic Snap player if I didn't select Shang-Chi as soon as the opportunity presented itself. This Shang-Chi control set was accompanied by Star-Lord and The Punisher. While I didn't think those cards went together, it was the actual draft portion where I would get to flesh out this deck.

The actual draft portion presents players with three cards to select from, continuing on until a ten-card deck has been assembled. In many cases, players will select from vanilla versions of cards, which have been separated into rarities. It'll be tempting to pass up cards with Epic and Legendary rarities, especially during rounds where every selection features a special buff. That buff could include a reduced Cost, an increased Power stat, or a bonus Quickdraw effect, just to name a few possibilities.

Decks assembled during a Draft will not follow the typical Marvel Snap meta. For many players, that's going to be the new mode's most alluring feature. Those who have grown tired of seeing whatever deck is dominating Untapped are, more often than not, going to see something wildly different. This is a mode that's all about testing a player's deck-building skills with whatever limited selections are available to them. After each game, players will get to upgrade their deck in different ways. That'll include picking cards to fill the deck to the usual 12-card amount, as well as picking Augments for their existing cards. Once I was presented a double On Reveal Augment option for my Shang-Chi, I was ready to live up to my most toxic potential.

The cream of the crop will ride their choices to five wins before accruing two losses, with an option to use a Respawn token to stay alive after the second loss. Once the run ends, the player will receive a slew of in-game rewards. The amount of goodies that I got for finishing with five wins was more than I expected. I received Bits for the Draft shop, XP for the Event Pass (which will operate similarly to Event Passes for other game modes), a Mystery Variant, Boosters, and another Draft ticket to play again. Just like other limited-time modes like Grand Arena, players will have a set number of Draft tickets, but that number will refresh over time.

As somebody who has admittedly gone through the motions with Marvel Snap's standard game mode, Draft mode put an extra spring in my step. The game felt fresh again. The only disappointment is knowing that it'll only be around for a limited time. This is something I want to see as a permanent feature, a mode that could complement standard play similar to what Arena does for Hearthstone , an idea that the Second Dinner team should be fairly familiar with.

Marvel Snap's Draft mode will go live later today and will stay active until September 8. Enjoy while it's around, but even after it's gone, expect it to stay in the LTM rotation, like High Voltage and Sanctum Showdown before it.

This preview is based on a Steam beta branch build provided by the developers.

items.title: MARVEL SNAP Draft Hands-On Preview – Here For A Good Time
items.summary: MARVEL SNAP’s new Draft Mode is a refreshing addition, but it would likely take much more to revitalize the game as a whole.
items.content:
Released on mobile and PC (early access) in the fall of 2022, MARVEL SNAP is a digital collectible card game and the brainchild of former Hearthstone game director Ben Brode , and Second Dinner, the studio he founded after leaving Blizzard. Upon its release, MARVEL SNAP proved not only to be a critical darling, winning Best Mobile Game at The Game Awards in 2022, but also immensely popular with players, becoming the top-grossing digital trading card game by September 2023, according to Forbes .

I, myself, was completely enamoured with it and played it roughly every day, racking up countless hours on mobile and around 38 hours on Steam. Furthermore, in December 2022, I wrote about the best decks to try – that article is long outdated, of course, but for a taste of what players were concocting at the time, you may find it here .

However, a few years on, MARVEL SNAP finds itself, for a myriad of reasons , in the difficult situation of having lost 75% of its revenue in 2025 and, presumably, a significant chunk of its player base, too. In an effort to revitalise the game, Second Dinner is finally adding a game mode that fans have been asking for ever since launch: Draft. Like in many other card games, digital or otherwise, MARVEL SNAP ’s Draft mode will have players build temporary decks from random selections of cards.

Unlike other card games, though, there is also a roguelike element at play here, with cards being able to be “augmented” after each round. Depending on the buffs available, Black Panther, for example, can have his power doubled a second time, which can be extremely valuable. Because of this, having good synergy not just between the cards themselves but the augments, as well, becomes crucial to securing a win. Each individual win will be rewarded, but getting to 5 wins will grant an additional Draft ticket alongside currency rewards. Drafts can go on for a maximum of 6 rounds, with players allowed to lose just the single time before proceedings come to a close.

Earlier this month, courtesy of the MARVEL SNAP developers, I was invited to a preview session in which they told me about what it took for them to bring Draft to their game, culminating in me getting some hands-on time with this new game mode. From the get-go, the team at Second Dinner mentioned that Draft is probably the most requested feature and that they’ve wanted to implement it in the game for a long time.

Because of the way that MARVEL SNAP is put together, specifically with regard to card rarity, they spoke about how difficult it was to implement the mode but that, ultimately, they are incredibly confident in this latest iteration of Draft, which has been in the works for the past year or so. Their hope is that Draft becomes a mainstay for both returning and perhaps especially new players, since no pre-existing card collection is needed to get the most out of it.

Unfortunately, Draft itself isn’t here to stay, as it will only be a limited game mode in MARVEL SNAP , running from the 24th of August at noon PT until the 7th of September at noon PT. This is disappointing, definitely, but my impression is that the team is more than open to bringing it back, potentially with a new pool of cards, if player reception is positive.

For what it’s worth, based on my time playing and winning 5 rounds of Draft, they absolutely should, as this is a good game mode which, with a bit more love and polish, could become one of the main reasons players are picking up MARVEL SNAP in the first place.

My hope is that things work out and that Draft makes a tangible impact on MARVEL SNAP , but if it only runs for the limited period specified above, my fear is that it won’t get the time to do so. I certainly won’t be back if Draft is here for a good time, not a long time.

BUILD! BUFF! BATTLE!

The most requested mode in MARVEL SNAP history has arrived. Draft drops you into a brand-new way to build: no collection, no pre-made decks, just you, a fresh set of cards, and the Augments to turn them into something wild. Here is everything you need to know before your first run.

WHAT IS DRAFT?

It's MARVEL SNAP meets draft style deck building, meets roguelike style upgrades! MARVEL SNAP Draft does not depend on your collection - you can draft from any available cards in the mode. Then, you get to flex your skills and adjust on the fly with Augments that add cool abilities, or leverage Stat Boosts that help you fight for priority.

WHY PLAY DRAFT?

Big Potential: Decks in Draft have more potential than ever, melding the excitement of a limited environment with the high-power potential of a roguelike. Always Fresh: Augments allow you to add abilities to cards to create unique abilities you've never seen in a normal SNAP game! Level Playing Field: Everyone can enjoy Draft whether you've been playing for years or just started yesterday, no collection required.

HOW DO YOU PLAY DRAFT?

Build your deck, take it to battle, secure two out of three Locations after turn 6, and DOMINATE the Draft on your way to 5 wins. It starts with your choice of 3 core stacks of cards. Pick between them to set the foundation of your deck. Add on to your core by drafting one of three cards until you fill out your initial 10 card deck. After each game, you'll get a chance to add to your deck or buff your cards with Augments. You can have a Black Panther with an additional doubling of Power, or a Wolverine that also destroys another card to get stronger! Sounds wild, right? Each win will be rewarded, but getting to 5 wins will grant you an additional entry ticket, a once per day bonus of a PMV, and other awesome rewards. Watch out though, 2 losses and it's back to the drafting board.

WHAT ARE AUGMENTS?

Augments are abilities you can apply to cards that add additional effects. If you're lucky, you'll even get an opportunity to Draft cards straight into your deck with Augments. They let you make super strong plays, and you can even put multiple Augments on the same card!

WHAT ARE STAT BOOSTS?

Unlike Augments, which fundamentally alter the nature of a card beyond just the numbers on it, Stat Boosts make cards cheaper or stronger. Sometimes, you'll get a Vision that costs 4, or has 11 power - that's a Stat Boost in action!

HOW LONG WILL MARVEL SNAP DRAFT BE HERE?

Draft will be available through September 8th at server reset. The shop will remain open for an additional 48 hours after the mode has ended to ensure there is ample time to maximize your currency. If you can't get enough Draft, be on the lookout for surveys where you'll get to tell us about your experience (and maybe even encourage the team to bring it back super fast).

DRAFT LOGIN REWARDS

We've already announced the first 3 decks in our Fractured Frontier Blog, but now it's time to celebrate Draft by announcing 2 MORE decks! A Mister Negative deck that inverts costs to make wild combos, and a Victoria Hand deck that boosts your created cards. That's right, we're putting 5 complete decks in login bonuses that are available to EVERYONE. Yes, everyone. Login ➡ get rewarded. This will happen over two different login events covering Aug 24 - Sep 6th, and Sep 7th - Sep 28th.

items.content:
on Google Preferred Source Google News Link copied to clipboard By Tomas Franzese Published Aug 22, 2026, 1:18 PM EDT News Marvel Snap's Draft mode finally arrives on Monday

Image: Second Dinner Marvel SNAP Sign in to your Polygon.com account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google News Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap After years of clamoring from its player base, Marvel Snap will finally get a Draft mode on Aug. 24.

Draft will be a limited-time game mode that will heavily modify the standard gameplay loops of the Marvel Comics-inspired collectible card game. An exclusive preview and interview with GameSpot detailed what Marvel Snap players can expect from Draft. Matches begin with players choosing a starter set that gives them three cards that fit different deck archetypes like destroy, ramp, move, or ongoing.

Players then draft seven more cards, which have modified cost or power stats specific to this mode or have "augments" that give them additional abilities. From there, players have to win five rounds of Draft to claim victory, building up their deck with two more cards (and more augments) over time.

Developer Sam Stoddard explained that the radical gameplay changes required for Draft are part of the reason it took so long for Second Dinner to make the mode. That's also why it's starting as a limited-time game mode and not a whole new permanent part of the game.

"Snap has a much lower number of cards, you have very small decks, so even the amount of variance you get isn’t super high, as well as the synergy is very high. There’s all these things that were really working against it, and it’s part of why it took so long to eventually get to a place where we were really happy with what we had as an offering," Stoddard explained to GameSpot. "And so part of the LTGM thing is that we have a lot of known unknowns right now. I enjoy the mode a lot, but I designed it. I’ve talked to a lot of other people who enjoy it, but we definitely need to really stress test it with a much larger group of people."

While there might be some issues that still need to be worked out, Draft mode is one of the most exciting updates for the game since its 2022 launch. Nearly four years and several controversies later , Marvel Snap maintains a passionate community and player base, with the game still receiving a brand-new card every single week. It's my favorite mobile game, and one of my favorite Marvel games in general, so I'm very happy to see the mode finally arrive.

Draft will arrive in the Android, iOS, and Windows PC versions of Marvel Snap on Aug. 24. As for when it'll return once this initial event concludes, Stoddard says that's something Second Dinner "will be trying to figure out from all that data," but that it won't "be too long before it comes back because we definitely have a lot of things that we want to try out."

The wilderness is calling. A whole new frontier unfolds across MARVEL SNAP as we ride into Earth-383. Gunslingers stalk the wasteland and every dusty crossroads hides new cards, locations, and events. New faces (and a few old ones) are drawing steel across the roster, two new locations are riding onto the map, and a full calendar of events guarantees there's always another showdown waiting. Let's take a quick look at what's coming in the Fractured Frontier season!

WEB SHOP BONUS

Purchase the Premium or Super Premium Season Pass on shop.marvelsnap.com and unlock AWESOME bonuses, including a Series 5 SNAP Pack and more. To ensure you get your rewards:

  • Log in to the game during the new season

    [/*]

  • Log in to the Web Shop and purchase the Premium or Super Premium Pass

    [/*]

  • Reload your SNAP client and claim your new rewards

    [/*]

Upgrading from Premium → Super Premium will NOT trigger the bonus. You must purchase the pass directly through the Web Shop.

NEW KEYWORD: QUICKDRAW

Quickdraw: These effects are active the first turn you draw them. (Next turn if cards are already revealing.) Say hello to Quickdraw, a new keyword that rewards drawing the right card at the right time. A card's Quickdraw effect becomes active on the turn you draw it, or on the following turn if cards have already started revealing, giving every draw the potential to change your plans. Example: Draw Psylocke Fractured Frontier at the perfect moment to discount your entire hand, or let Jane Foster Fractured Frontier judge the worthy a second time. items.title: Critics week: Marvel Snap thrills by turning its players into game designers
items.summary: Legendary games writer and author Christian Donlan says the genius of Second Dinner’s card battler is in how it turns players into creators.
items.content:
We’re trying something a bit different this week. We asked five game critics for a piece on a mobile game they play regularly, but never get to actually write about .

Our final piece is from legendary games writer and author Christian Donlan:

Every now and then I find myself wondering about my Desert Island Games list, and if Marvel Snap would be in it. I’m increasingly certain that it would be. Marvel Snap’s a collectible card game made by some of the developers behind that other collectible card game Hearthstone. I loved Hearthstone for a bit, but I eventually felt left behind by the meta. I’d join a game and wouldn’t have much of an idea of what was going on.

Marvel Snap, however, is something I’ve stuck with pretty much since the launch. I don’t know if I’m good at it. I suspect I’m actually pretty bad at it. And yet it’s the first thing I fire up on my phone every morning. Sometimes, it’s the last thing I see before I put my phone down at night.

And this is weird. It’s weird for two reasons. The first is that I’ve always suspected I’m a bit too thick for CCGs. I like collecting things and unlocking things, but the part of my brain I need to plan combos and think about synergies isn’t really there when I call on it. I don’t know if you’ve ever seen a magician handle a deck of cards and briefly transform them into a living thing as they spring around and snap from one delicate hand to the next? And then you hold the deck yourself and it’s just: who killed this thing? The whole deck’s suddenly shockingly inert? It’s the same situation for me with combos. Other players can use them. But when I get my opening deal, I’m in plodder mode. I can play one card and then another, but the relationships between cards do not easily speak to me.

The second reason is a lot simpler: I don’t know very much about Marvel. So the rich tradition and storied lore that Marvel Snap builds on is largely missing for me. I had to look up Mysterio to see why his card conjures illusions. I had never heard of Agatha Harkness – my favourite card in the deck but I’d need 3000 words and a white board to explain why – before she became a staple of my starting hand. (A clever friend once leant me the Matt Fraction and David Aja run of Hawkeye, and I thought it was luminously good, but I don’t play Hawkeye in my deck in Marvel Snap, not even out of solidarity, so it doesn’t help much in terms of orientation.)

Here is the thing, though. None of those reasons for not clicking with Marvel Snap really matter. I have clicked. And I continue to click. And I think the reason is actually pretty simple. Beyond being colourful and fun and lively, beyond having short matches and decks of just 12 cards, so that even I have the brain space to put something interesting together, Marvel Snap gets at something deeper, richer and also simpler. It reminds me of how much fun game design must be. To play Marvel Snap is to feel a bit like a game designer yourself.

And this in turn is because of the cards – those beautiful, intriguing, playful cards. Marvel Snap tasks you and a rival with playing cards across three locations, with the mana rising each turn, which means that you can play increasingly powerful cards as the game progresses. If you win two of the three locations by the end of the sixth round, you win the match. So the agenda is both extremely simple and has a decent amount of leeway to it. You can really biff one location – reader, I often do – and still scrape by on the others and win. There’s a bit of gamesmanship to it as well because of those three locations. It’s not just about guessing what your opponent is going to play, but where.

All fine. But if it wasn’t for the cards, none of this would be worth talking about. And the cards properly sing. Like a lot of CCGs, Marvel snap has decent straight-ahead attack cards, and it has cards that do cool things like give you more mana, that boost other cards in interesting ways, and that change up locations and location powers and maybe even grant players a seventh round. All fine. But then it has the cards that do things where you read the text and go: huh. How is that going to work? What does that even do?!

To keep this brief I will give you just two short examples. Or perhaps it’s one example that isn’t so short.

Captain Marvel (no idea, I’m aware there was a movie) is a decent power card, but her big trick is that at the end of the game, if she can move to a location that wins the game for you she will. I love this. I don’t even have to be semi-competent and if I’m playing the Captain, maybe I’ll sneak a win. But then there’s this other card, Martyr (really no idea about this one, and I’m pretty sure there hasn’t been a movie) who is low cost but high power, and at the end of the game if you’re winning, she can move to a location that will lose you the game.

The gamble, obviously, is that you’re getting a lot of power for a little cost with Martyr, and you just have to hope that she doesn’t erupt at the end and ruin everything. But for me, when I saw Martyr, who can’t wait to lose things for you, and I was already used to playing Captain Marvel, who does the absolute opposite, I started thinking: what happens if you play them both together? At the end of the game one is zinging off to win, and the other is zinging off to lose. How does the game cope with that? Does your phone just suddenly explode?

What happens is…well, I won’t spoil it. And it doesn’t actually matter what happens. What matters is that the game pushed me towards thinking of some truly braintwisting possible mechanics just because the design was so outré I had to dig into it. For a few days, while I was really experimenting with Martyr and Captain Marvel, I felt like I was a designer. I felt like I was painting with cards and numbers and abilities.

This is exactly what keeps me playing. It keeps me experimenting with the cards I know and longing for the cards I don’t have yet. I’ve spent a fair amount of money on Snap over the years – only through the Battle Pass equivalent, because it’s less like spending money and more like making a donation in order to get a bunch of Christmas presents – and it’s partly because I like to earn certain cards a little quicker, but mainly because I feel like the core, free game is generous and playful and makes me think so much, so I want to chuck the developers some money for that. This is probably the best case scenario for a free-to-play game if you ask me. You pay now and then because you want to say thank you to these people who have given you so much joy.

items.content:
Assemble your Avengers and swing out your Spiders because it’s time to fight for supremacy and decide which team will rise to the top. Welcome to TEAM CLASH, MARVEL SNAP’s newest limited time game mode!

What is Team Clash?

Team Clash is the BRAND NEW game mode that lets you command a team of your favorite characters. There are a total of five teams in this mode and each brings their own unique ability that creates all new synergies and play lines. The new team abilities make sure that you’re leveraging each team’s powerful abilities by using members of the same team.  Additionally, each of the six core characters on each team has their own new unique ability, so when you see the Team Clash logo above their name and unique Team Clash Border on a card, there is a brand new ability that exists only in Team Clash. Characters that share the same team affiliation will be marked with the team logo on the top left corner. 

How do you play?

Start your Team Clash journey by selecting one of five main teams. Each team includes a unique ability that will help boost the abilities or power of your characters in that team. Six of the cards in the deck will be locked to the pre-designated characters, but you will have the option to customize the other 6 cards for the deck with your own collection of cards. 

Once the match begins, everything plays out in classic SNAP fashion, but your team’s mechanics and new character skills will provide opportunities for new play lines and synergies.

From adamantium nightmares to shattered memories and uncontrollable fury, this season embraces the darker side of mutation, where heroes are made, remade, and rebuilt against their will. The labs might be cold, but the rewards aren’t. Purchase the Premium or Super Premium Season Pass on shop.marvelsnap.com and unlock AWESOME bonuses, including a Colleen Wing variant from Hyeonsick Choi and three Wrapping Paper Borders. items.content:
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

(Image credit: Wizards of the Coast / Square Enix / Wisnu Tan / Second Dinner / Shutterstock / ex_artist) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Threads Email Share this article 1 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter For some time, Marvel Snap was the only digital card game I could stomach. It was, and in many ways still is, a prime example of what the genre should be.

This game could not be physical. Each match relies too heavily on randomly selected locations and card effects, which (at times) would be impossible to track with cardboard and dice.

But it's also simply an exhilarating experience at its core.

The bombastic gameplay is constructed with precise deck building, in-the-moment strategizing, and a healthy dose of luck (a key tenant of any good card game) that I frankly couldn't get enough of.

As is so often true of gaming in the modern era, I've felt my desire to play Snap wane in recent weeks (just like many others) because of monetization. For the first time in well over a year, I have yet to purchase this month's season pass (and currently have no plans to), nor grinded my way to the top player tier (Infinite).

Mark Rosewater has made me excited for Magic's next Universes Beyond set I vowed never to buy a PS5 but changed my mind, and I don't miss my gaming PC Mystery Booster Commander Edition could be the best game I’ll never play I don’t mind some monetization, and generally, Marvel Snap has handled things well. There have been plenty of free-to-play ways to earn its premium currency (Gold) so you can purchase cosmetics (such as alternate artwork for your cards), and the only card locked behind a paywall each month was the Season Pass card – and it would become free to earn the following month.

However, subtle frustrations have been growing. There have become steadily fewer ways to earn Gold simply by playing the game and its events, there have been leaked datamined plans for the upgraded Super Premium Season Pass to include its own exclusive game piece (meaning two cards will be stuck behind a paywall each month), and during the recent High Voltage Overdrive event, the top prize was practically impossible to win without using Gold.

Some Reddit users did manage to play enough to earn this card (Kid Omega) simply by playing a lot, but to get a sense of how difficult this feat is, this player apparently played 42 hours and 38 minutes of Marvel Snap during the event and still had to dish out 100 Gold to afford the card.

For further context: previous events had, at worst, allowed you to unlock a greater range of rewards with paid currency. You could always unlock the top prize (or even a few of the top prizes) simply by playing a reasonable amount and spending your winnings wisely – and some events would reward players with every prize if they played enough, no purchase necessary.

Before you go to the comments below, I’m well aware that spending money on game pieces isn’t an unheard-of concept in card games. For many TCGs, it's a core principle.

World of Warcraft is coming to D&D — it’s bringing Universes Beyond with it Apple Arcade is a joyful reminder of when mobile gaming was about fun, not emptying your wallet I played all 279 Apple Arcade games — here are the eight best, from genius quick puzzlers to addictive life sims With Marvel Snap , however, my and others’ frustration comes from how the situation has changed so drastically from where the game began.
